notes:
Task and constraints: Choose the maximum number of pairs that can form a chain, requiring each selected pair's first value to exceed the previous pair's second value.
Idea: `findLongestChain` sorts `pairs` by their second coordinate and accepts a pair whenever its first coordinate is greater than `last`.
Technique and why it applies: Earliest-finish-time greedy is optimal because ending as early as possible leaves the largest feasible range for later pairs; `last` records the chosen chain's endpoint.
Invariant: After each accepted pair, `last` is the second coordinate of the most recently selected pair, and `count` is the length of the greedy chain.
Edge cases: Empty input returns zero; equal or overlapping boundaries are rejected by the strict `a > last` condition.
Complexity: Sorting takes O(n log n) time and the scan takes O(n), for O(n log n) total time and O(1) auxiliary space beyond the in-place sort.
complexity_reason: Sorting by the second coordinate makes each accepted pair finish as early as possible, so the scan is linear after sorting.

notes:
Task and constraints: Find the longest chain of integer pairs where each next pair starts strictly after the previous pair ends.
Idea: `findLongestChain` sorts `p` by `a[1]`, then greedily accepts each `x` whose first value exceeds `last`.
Technique and why it applies: The earliest-ending interval greedy choice preserves the most room for future pairs and is optimal for this chain condition.
Invariant: `last` is the ending value of the latest accepted pair; `count` counts exactly the accepted pairs.
Edge cases: An empty array returns zero; equal boundaries do not chain because the comparison is strict.
Complexity: Sorting costs O(n log n), scanning costs O(n), and the algorithm uses O(1) auxiliary state apart from sorting implementation details.
complexity_reason: The comparator orders pairs by their end values, and each scan step checks one candidate in constant time.

notes:
Task and constraints: Count every non-empty palindromic substring of `s`, including distinct occurrences with identical text.
Idea: `countSubstrings` considers both odd centers `(c,c)` and even centers `(c,c+1)` and expands outward while characters match.
Technique and why it applies: Every palindrome has a center of one of those two forms, so expansion enumerates all palindromic intervals without storing substrings.
Invariant: Each successful expansion corresponds to one palindrome and increments `ans` exactly once.
Edge cases: Empty strings return zero; one-character strings contribute one palindrome per character; even-length palindromes require the gap centers.
Complexity: There are O(n) centers and each expansion can span O(n), giving O(n²) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
complexity_reason: Each of the roughly two centers per character can expand across the string in the worst case.

notes:
Task and constraints: Count all palindromic substring occurrences in `s`, considering both odd and even lengths.
Idea: `countSubstrings` calls `expand` for `(c,c)` and `(c,c+1)` at every character position.
Technique and why it applies: Center expansion tests matching symmetric characters and counts each valid interval, avoiding a quadratic substring table.
Invariant: `expand` returns the number of palindromes with its chosen center; the outer method sums the disjoint center-based counts.
Edge cases: Empty input returns zero; mismatched neighbors stop an expansion immediately; even palindromes are found only by gap centers.
Complexity: O(n) centers each perform up to O(n) comparisons, so time is O(n²) and auxiliary space is O(1).
complexity_reason: The helper advances both endpoints only while they remain in bounds and their characters match.

notes:
Task and constraints: Replace each sentence word with its shortest dictionary root prefix, or leave the word unchanged if none matches.
Idea: `replaceWords` stores `dictionary` in `roots`, then tests prefixes from length one upward for each word and takes the first match.
Technique and why it applies: Increasing prefix length guarantees the first set hit is the shortest valid root; the set provides expected constant-time membership checks.
Invariant: Each appended output token is either the shortest matching root found so far for that word or the original word when no root matches.
Edge cases: Words without any root remain unchanged; a root equal to the whole word is valid; splitting and joining preserve ordinary space-separated sentence words.
Complexity: Prefix construction and hashing take expected time proportional to the total characters examined; worst-case repeated slicing and hashing can make time O(sum of word lengths squared), with O(total input size) storage for roots and output.
complexity_reason: The prefix loop stops at its first set match, but slicing and hashing longer prefixes may revisit characters.

notes:
Task and constraints: Substitute the shortest dictionary root at the beginning of each sentence word, retaining words with no matching root.
Idea: `replaceWords` builds `roots` as a `HashSet`; for each `w`, it checks `substring(0,i)` in increasing `i` order and stops at the first hit.
Technique and why it applies: Prefixes tested from shortest to longest ensure minimal-root selection, while hash lookups avoid scanning every dictionary entry.
Invariant: `root` remains the original word until a matching prefix is found, then holds the shortest prefix discovered.
Edge cases: No matching prefix leaves `w` unchanged; duplicate dictionary roots collapse harmlessly in the set; empty sentence behavior depends on Java's `split` semantics.
Complexity: Set construction uses O(total dictionary characters) space; substring creation and hashing can yield O(sum of squared word lengths) worst-case time, with output storage proportional to sentence length.
complexity_reason: Testing prefixes in ascending length guarantees the selected root is the first and therefore shortest match.

notes:
Task and constraints: Simulate senator bans in circular order and return the party that eventually has senators remaining.
Idea: `predictPartyVictory` stores each party's indices in deques; it pops the earliest Radiant and Dire indices, and requeues the earlier senator at index plus `n`.
Technique and why it applies: Queue order represents the next available senator in each party; adding `n` models that senator's next turn after one full cycle.
Invariant: Each queue contains the surviving senators of one party in increasing future-turn order.
Edge cases: If the input contains only one party, the opposing queue is initially empty and that party wins; each round removes one senator permanently.
Complexity: Each senator is requeued at most once per round until the other party is exhausted, giving O(n) time and O(n) space.
complexity_reason: Each round removes one senator from each party and requeues only the earlier index shifted by one cycle.

notes:
Task and constraints: Determine whether Radiant or Dire wins the circular banning process represented by `s`.
Idea: `predictPartyVictory` puts each senator index into `r` or `d`, then repeatedly removes their heads and re-adds the earlier index plus `n`.
Technique and why it applies: Two FIFO queues preserve each party's turn order; adding `n` schedules a surviving senator in the next cycle.
Invariant: Queue heads are the next eligible senators from each party, and all queued indices are in future-turn order.
Edge cases: An input with only R or only D skips the loop and returns that party; each duel permanently eliminates one senator.
Complexity: Queue operations are constant time and at most O(n) eliminations occur, so total time is O(n) and space is O(n).
complexity_reason: The two queues preserve turn order while shifted indices model the next circular pass without simulating empty turns.

notes:
Task and constraints: Minimize copy-all and paste operations to reach exactly `n` characters starting from one character.
Idea: `minSteps` repeatedly divides `n` by each factor `p`, adding `p` for every occurrence, then adds any remaining prime factor.
Technique and why it applies: The optimal operation count equals the sum of prime factors with multiplicity, because each factor-sized growth stage costs that factor's copy/paste operations.
Invariant: After processing a divisor, `ans` contains the sum of extracted prime factors and the remaining `n` has no copies of that divisor.
Edge cases: For `n == 1`, the loop is skipped and zero operations are returned; a final `n > 1` is a remaining prime factor.
Complexity: Trial division checks factors up to the square root of the shrinking value, giving O(sqrt n) time in the stated bound and O(1) auxiliary space.
complexity_reason: Repeatedly extracting prime factors accounts for every required multiplication stage, including a final unpaired prime factor.

notes:
Task and constraints: Compute the minimum copy-all and paste operations required to grow one character into exactly `n` characters.
Idea: `minSteps` tests divisors `p`, repeatedly divides out each factor, and accumulates that factor in `ans`.
Technique and why it applies: Prime-factor decomposition minimizes the sum of factor-sized operation stages; any remaining value above one is prime and contributes itself.
Invariant: After each division, `n` is the unprocessed factor remainder and `ans` is the sum of factors already removed with multiplicity.
Edge cases: `n == 1` returns zero; repeated prime factors are added repeatedly; the loop condition avoids testing divisors beyond the square root of the current remainder.
Complexity: Trial division runs in O(sqrt n) time in the worst case and stores only scalar variables, so auxiliary space is O(1).
complexity_reason: The loop accumulates each repeated prime divisor, then adds the remaining prime when necessary.

notes:
Task and constraints: Return one node for each distinct subtree shape and value pattern that occurs at least twice.
Idea: `dfs` recursively obtains left and right subtree IDs, interns `(n.val,left_id,right_id)` in `ids`, and counts each resulting ID.
Technique and why it applies: Canonical structural tuples give identical subtrees the same identifier; appending a node only when its count reaches two avoids duplicate output roots.
Invariant: Every completed subtree has an ID uniquely representing its value and ordered child structures, and `counts[i]` records how many times that structure was seen.
Edge cases: `None` maps to ID zero; a repeated subtree is appended only on its second occurrence, not every later occurrence.
Complexity: Each node is processed once with expected constant-time dictionary operations, giving O(n) expected time and O(n) space for IDs, counts, and recursion.
complexity_reason: Interning each value-and-child-ID tuple makes structural equality a dictionary lookup instead of repeated subtree comparison.

notes:
Task and constraints: Find one root reference for every subtree structure that appears more than once in the binary tree.
Idea: `dfs` serializes a node as its value and the IDs of its left and right children, interns that string in `ids`, and updates `counts`.
Technique and why it applies: Canonical serialization maps equal subtrees to the same ID; adding to `out` only when a count becomes two returns each duplicate structure once.
Invariant: `ids` maps each canonical node/child representation to a stable ID, while `counts` records occurrences of that ID.
Edge cases: Null children return ID zero; later occurrences beyond the second do not append another root; tree recursion depth follows tree height.
Complexity: Expected O(n) time for `n` nodes with hash maps and O(n) space for serialization keys, counts, output, and recursion.
complexity_reason: Every node's canonical key is built from child IDs already computed by postorder recursion.

notes:
Task and constraints: Decide whether two distinct BST nodes sum to `k`; the pair must use separate node visits.
Idea: `findTarget` performs DFS and checks whether `k - n.val` is already in `seen` before adding the current value.
Technique and why it applies: A hash set of previously visited values makes each complement check expected O(1), without needing to rely on BST ordering.
Invariant: Before adding `n.val`, `seen` contains exactly the values of nodes visited earlier, so a match always pairs the current node with a distinct earlier node.
Edge cases: A null node returns false; a node cannot pair with itself because its value is inserted only after the lookup; duplicate values at distinct nodes can form a valid pair.
Complexity: Each node is visited at most once, giving O(n) expected time and O(n) auxiliary space.
complexity_reason: Checking the complement before insertion prevents a single node from satisfying the target with itself.

notes:
Task and constraints: Return true if two distinct nodes in the BST add to target `k`.
Idea: `findTarget` calls `dfs`; each visit checks `s.contains(k - n.val)`, adds `n.val`, and explores left or right recursively.
Technique and why it applies: Complement lookup in a `HashSet` detects a prior partner in expected constant time and works regardless of traversal order.
Invariant: The set contains values from nodes visited earlier, and the current node is tested before it is added.
Edge cases: Null nodes return false; lookup-before-add prevents pairing a node with itself; short-circuit `||` stops after a successful match.
Complexity: Each node is visited at most once, so expected time is O(n) and the set plus recursion uses O(n) space.
complexity_reason: The complement is checked before adding the current value, enforcing that the matching nodes are distinct.

notes:
Task and constraints: Build a maximum binary tree where each segment's maximum becomes its root and the left/right segments form its children.
Idea: `constructMaximumBinaryTree` finds the maximum index `i`, creates `TreeNode(nums[i])`, and recursively builds from `nums[:i]` and `nums[i+1:]`.
Technique and why it applies: The maximum element uniquely determines the root for each segment, and recursive subsegments preserve the required in-order array order.
Invariant: Each recursive call returns the maximum-tree representation of exactly its input slice.
Edge cases: An empty slice returns `None`; a strictly increasing or decreasing array can produce a skewed tree and deepest recursion.
Complexity: Finding each segment maximum and slicing can sum to O(n²) time; recursion and slice allocations require O(n) worst-case auxiliary space in addition to the output tree.
complexity_reason: Repeated maximum scans cost quadratic time on monotonic inputs, and Python slicing copies each recursive subarray.

notes:
Task and constraints: Construct a maximum binary tree from `a`, recursively using each segment's largest value as its root.
Idea: `constructMaximumBinaryTree` calls `build(a,0,a.length)`; `build` scans `[l,r)` for the maximum index and recurses on both sides.
Technique and why it applies: The segment maximum determines the root, and half-open index ranges avoid allocating copied subarrays while preserving left-to-right structure.
Invariant: `build(a,l,r)` returns the maximum tree containing exactly the values in that half-open range.
Edge cases: An empty range returns null; monotonic input can create a skewed tree; the scan uses strict `>` so the first maximum is retained if values tie.
Complexity: Repeated scans take O(n²) worst-case time, while recursion uses O(h) stack space, up to O(n) for a skewed tree.
complexity_reason: The index-range recursion avoids array copies but still rescans every segment to locate its maximum.

notes:
Task and constraints: Return whether the sequence of U, D, L, and R moves ends at the origin.
Idea: `judgeCircle` compares the number of U moves with D and the number of L moves with R.
Technique and why it applies: Each opposite direction cancels one unit of displacement, so equal counts on both axes are equivalent to returning to the start.
Invariant: The final position is the origin exactly when vertical and horizontal move counts balance independently.
Edge cases: Empty moves return true; any unknown character would be ignored by these `count` checks rather than validated.
Complexity: Each `count` scans the string, and four scans remain O(n) total time with O(1) auxiliary space.
complexity_reason: Four linear character counts determine whether both displacement axes cancel without allocating coordinate state.

notes:
Task and constraints: Determine whether a robot returns to its starting point after reading the move string `s`.
Idea: `judgeCircle` updates `x` and `y` for U, D, L, and R, then tests whether both are zero.
Technique and why it applies: Accumulating signed displacement directly models the robot's position and opposing moves cancel naturally.
Invariant: After each character, `(x,y)` equals the net horizontal and vertical displacement of the processed prefix.
Edge cases: Empty input returns true; the final `else` treats any character other than U, D, or L as a right move, so correctness assumes valid R/U/D/L input.
Complexity: The loop processes each character once for O(n) time and uses O(1) auxiliary space.
complexity_reason: The single pass updates two integer coordinates, so runtime grows linearly and memory remains constant.

notes:
Task and constraints: Replace each image cell with the floor of the average of itself and all in-bounds cells in its surrounding 3-by-3 neighborhood.
Idea: `imageSmoother` creates `out`, clips row and column ranges with `max` and `min`, collects valid `vals`, and stores `sum(vals)//len(vals)`.
Technique and why it applies: Clipping the neighborhood at matrix boundaries excludes nonexistent cells, and integer floor division implements the required floor average.
Invariant: Every output cell is computed solely from the unchanged input matrix, preventing earlier smoothed values from affecting later results.
Edge cases: Corner and edge cells have fewer neighbors; the stated implementation assumes a non-empty rectangular matrix.
Complexity: Each cell examines at most nine values, so time is O(mn); the output matrix and temporary neighborhood list use O(mn) total extra space, with O(1) temporary list size per cell.
complexity_reason: The nested loops visit each cell once and inspect no more than nine input positions.

notes:
Task and constraints: Smooth every cell by flooring the average of that cell and its valid neighbors in the surrounding 3-by-3 area.
Idea: `imageSmoother` loops over all cells, bounds neighbor indices using `Math.max` and `Math.min`, accumulates `sum` and `count`, then stores integer division `sum/count`.
Technique and why it applies: The clipped loops handle borders naturally, and Java integer division floors the nonnegative average as required.
Invariant: The method reads exclusively from input `a` and writes to separate `out`, so each result uses original pixel values.
Edge cases: Corners and edges include fewer neighbors; implementation assumes `a` has at least one row and each row is non-empty and rectangular.
Complexity: At most nine neighbors are checked per cell, giving O(mn) time and O(mn) space for the output matrix.
complexity_reason: The fixed-size neighborhood bounds the work per pixel independently of matrix dimensions.
